A model attribution edit summary is `Content in this edit is translated from the existing German Wikipedia article at ; see its history for attribution.` * You may also add the template `{{Translated|de|Bundesautobahn 2}}` to the talk page. **Bundesautobahn 2** (translates from German as *Federal Motorway 2*, short form **Autobahn 2**, abbreviated as **BAB 2** or **A 2**) is an autobahn in Germany that connects the Ruhr area in the west to Berlin in the east. The A 2 starts at the junction with the A3 near the western city of Oberhausen, passes along the north side of the Ruhr valley, through the Münsterland and into Ostwestfalen, crossing the former inner German border and continuing through the Magdeburger Börde to merge into the Berliner Ring shortly before reaching Berlin.

title: German Language Levels Explained: A1 to C2
content: # German Language Levels Explained: A1 to C2. If you’ve ever searched for a German course and felt confused by the labels A1, A2, B1, B2, C1, and C2  you’re not alone. These are the official **German language levels** used worldwide to measure how well you understand, speak, read, and write German. They come from the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages or CEFR, and they apply to every learner from someone who just said their first *“Hallo”* to someone reading Goethe in the original. Before you invest time and money into learning, it helps to know exactly what each level means, what skills it builds, and how long it takes to get there. ## **What Is the CEFR and Why Does It Matter for German Learners?**. * **A (Basic User)** — A1 and A2. So whether you’re preparing for university admission, a work visa, or simply personal growth, your CEFR level is the universal currency of German learning.

title: German Two-Way Prepositions - German With Laura
content: # German Two-Way Prepositions. At this point in your German-learning journey, you’ve probably got a good sense for accusative and dative prepositions (<– if not, start there!). But now there’s a whole category of prepositions that switch back-and-forth between the accusative (when indicating direction) and dative (when indicating location)?! You already know how to use accusative and dative case declensions (<– or at least you should; read up on that first!). So, really, all you need is to study the list of two-way prepositions and check out some examples of when they’re used with the accusative and when with the dative. * **how to use the accusative or dative *cases* with two-way prepositions**. ## What are Two-Way Prepositions? But the trickier part is knowing when to use these two-way prepositions with a noun in the *accusative* case and when to use them with a noun in the *dative.*. ## When & How To Use Two-way Prepositions.
